headline: Does a college football win put votes on the scoreboard?
title: Irrelevant events affect voters’ evaluations of government performance
note: The authors matched local college football results with election returns. They estimated that a win in the ten days before an election gave the incumbent party an extra 1.61 percentage points of the local vote. Reanalysis: Fowler and Montagnes found that the original association failed several checks implied by the causal interpretation. A subsequent exchange disputed how to interpret the observational evidence. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1502615112 https://doi.org/10.1086/719636 https://doi.org/10.1086/722038

headline: Can your startle reflex give away your views on the death penalty?
title: Political Attitudes Vary with Physiological Traits
note: Researchers exposed 46 adults with strong political views to sudden noises and threatening images. They reported that people who reacted more strongly were more likely to favor policies such as capital punishment and higher defense spending. A preregistered direct replication and additional conceptual replications did not support the original physiology and ideology findings. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-020-0823-z

headline: Can a hand-sanitizer dispenser make you more conservative?
title: Dirty Liberals!: Reminders of Physical Cleanliness Influence Moral and Political Attitudes
note: Participants reporting their political views near a sanitizer dispenser were said to report more conservative attitudes than participants near a blank wall. Two replications of the dispenser experiment failed to reproduce the original result. A pooled analysis including a third failed replication estimated a very small effect. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspa0000238

headline: One glimpse of the US flag, eight months more Republican?
title: A Single Exposure to the American Flag Shifts Support Toward Republicanism up to 8 Months Later
note: During the 2008 US election, researchers briefly showed some participants an American flag. They reported greater Republican support in that group, with some attitude differences still visible eight months later. Many Labs tested the shorter-term Study 2 effect and found a near-zero result. The original team’s later meta-analysis found that estimates had declined toward zero. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000178 https://doi.org/10.1521/soco.2020.38.6.489

headline: Can two genes tell you whether someone will vote?
title: Two Genes Predict Voter Turnout
note: The authors linked turnout to a variant of MAOA and reported that a 5-HTT variant predicted turnout in combination with religious attendance. Reanalysis: Charney and English disputed the two-gene result. A later independent study reported support for the 5-HTT result using a new dataset. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055411000554 https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055413000087

headline: Can calling someone a voter instead of asking them to vote change whether they show up?
title: Motivating Voter Turnout by Invoking the Self
note: The researchers randomly varied noun and verb wording in questionnaires. In two field studies they matched respondents to official turnout records and reported higher turnout after the noun wording. A larger field replication found no detectable turnout advantage for the noun wording. The original team disputed the adequacy of some replication designs. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1513727113 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925985/

headline: Can telling men they scored like women make them more pro-war?
title: Overdoing Gender: A Test of the Masculine Overcompensation Thesis
note: Men given feedback that their gender-identity scores were in the feminine range subsequently reported greater support for war in a student experiment. Preregistered replication and extension: a national probability sample of 2,774 did not recover the original pattern across the political measures. https://doi.org/10.1017/XPS.2025.10027

headline: Could estimated fertility predict a vote for Obama?
title: Fertility and race perception predict voter preference for Barack Obama
note: The authors linked estimated conception risk and race perception to women’s candidate preferences in the 2008 US election. Preregistered conceptual replication: rated candidate preferences using a 2020 election scenario that included Obama. The original pattern did not recur. https://doi.org/10.1177/00332941241233209

headline: One more daughter, one more liberal vote in Congress?
title: Female Socialization: How Daughters Affect Their Legislator Fathers' Voting on Women's Issues
note: The author compared lawmakers with the same number of children. Those with more daughters tended to cast more liberal votes, especially on reproductive rights. Reanalysis and extension: Green et al. found no daughter effect in Congress before or after the original period. https://doi.org/10.1086/724744

headline: One second, two faces. Who's going to Congress?
title: Inferences of Competence from Faces Predict Election Outcomes
note: Participants looked at pairs of candidate photos and picked the person who looked more competent. In the 2004 US Senate races the authors examined, that pick matched the winner 68.8% of the time.

headline: Can unusual rainfall be used to estimate whether falling income makes civil conflict more likely?
title: Economic Shocks and Civil Conflict: An Instrumental Variables Approach
note: The authors used rainfall variation as an instrument for economic growth and related the estimated growth shocks to civil conflict in African countries.

headline: Can children pick an election winner by picking a boat captain?
title: Predicting Elections: Child’s Play!
note: After playing a game, children saw photos of two candidates and chose the one they wanted as their boat captain. Researchers compared their choices with the winners of the actual elections.

headline: Could a dopamine receptor variant predict ideology only for people with more friends?
title: Friendships Moderate an Association Between a Dopamine Gene Variant and Political Ideology
note: The authors modeled ideology as a function of a DRD4 variant, number of reported friends and their interaction. Their association depended on the number of friends.

headline: Can the number of taste buds on your tongue predict conservatism?
title: A matter of taste: Gustatory sensitivity predicts political ideology
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors reported associations between taste sensitivity and conservatism, including an association with the density of fungiform papillae.

headline: Do your biceps predict your views on redistribution?
title: The ancestral logic of politics: upper-body strength regulates men's assertion of self-interest over economic redistribution
note: The authors reported a relationship between men's upper-body strength and support for redistribution that varied with socioeconomic status.

headline: Can a flag you don't consciously see change your politics?
title: Subliminal exposure to national flags affects political thought and behavior
note: Experiments reported changes in political attitudes and voting behavior following briefly presented images of the Israeli flag.

headline: Can a 100-millisecond glance at candidates’ faces predict real election winners?
title: Predicting Political Elections From Rapid and Unreflective Face Judgments
note: Participants judged perceived competence from briefly shown face pairs. The authors compared those judgments with actual election outcomes.

headline: Can rain at a Tea Party rally predict how people vote more than a year later?
title: Do Political Protests Matter? Evidence From the Tea Party Movement
note: The researchers used rainfall on the day of coordinated rallies to estimate the effect of rally attendance on later political activity and Republican vote shares.

headline: Can your sweat response to disgusting pictures predict your politics?
title: Disgust sensitivity and the neurophysiology of left-right political orientations
note: The researchers related skin-conductance responses to disgust-inducing pictures to self-reported political views.

headline: Can a blank expression give away your politics?
title: Facial Recognition Technology and Human Raters Can Predict Political Orientation From Images of Expressionless Faces Even When Controlling for Demographics and Self-Presentation
note: In a follow-up to earlier profile-photo work, the authors used standardized, expressionless portraits. They reported that an algorithm and human raters could predict self-reported political orientation above chance in their sample.

headline: Do people who agree with you politically smell better?
title: Assortative Mating on Ideology Could Operate Through Olfactory Cues
note: Participants rated strangers' body odor. The authors reported that people preferred the scent of strangers whose political views were closer to their own and proposed that smell might play a part in choosing a partner.

headline: Can a portrait predict which Chinese officials get promoted or purged?
title: Portraits of Power: Facial Appearance and the Tacit Domain of Political Selection in China
note: The researchers trained a model to reproduce human judgments of facial appearance and applied it to portraits of more than 4,000 Chinese officials. Higher scores for looking competent or trustworthy tracked promotion and purge outcomes. The scores describe how faces are judged.

headline: Can cabinet ministers' faces be used to estimate how corrupt a country is?
title: Obesity of politicians and corruption in post-Soviet countries
venue: Economics of Transition and Institutional Change
note: A computer vision model estimated body mass index from 299 ministers' portraits in 15 post-Soviet states. The authors compared each cabinet's median estimated BMI with country-level corruption indices and proposed ministers' BMI as a proxy for political corruption.

headline: Can diplomats' parking tickets reveal the corruption norms of their home countries?
title: Corruption, Norms, and Legal Enforcement: Evidence from Diplomatic Parking Tickets
note: The authors linked United Nations diplomats' Manhattan parking violations to their home-country corruption scores and examined changes after enforcement tightened. They interpreted the cross-country relationship before enforcement as evidence about norms carried across borders.

headline: Can satellites tell whether a leader favors their own hometown?
title: Regional Favoritism
note: The authors compared satellite nighttime light intensity in leaders' birth regions during and outside their terms. They interpreted the increase in brightness during a leader's tenure as evidence of regional favoritism, using light as a proxy for local economic activity.

headline: Does El Niño double the risk of a new civil conflict in the tropics?
title: Civil conflicts are associated with the global climate
note: The researchers matched conflict onsets from 1950 to 2004 to phases of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation. They estimated roughly twice the probability of conflict onset in affected tropical countries in El Niño years versus La Niña years and used that comparison to estimate the possible contribution of ENSO to historical conflict.

headline: Can too much or too little rain explain killings of people accused of witchcraft?
title: Poverty and Witch Killing
note: Using village data from rural Tanzania, the study treated unusually low or high rainfall as a source of variation in income. The authors used its relationship to killings of people accused of witchcraft to infer an effect of income shocks.

headline: Can a predecessor's firstborn child help estimate whether queens went to war more than kings?
title: Queens
note: In historical European monarchies, the authors used the sex of a previous ruler's firstborn and whether that predecessor had a sister as instruments for queenly rule. They estimated higher war participation under queens and proposed differences in spouses' roles as an explanation.

headline: Does an older leader mean a greater risk of an international dispute?
title: Leader Age, Regime Type, and Violent International Relations
note: The study linked leaders' ages to dispute initiation and escalation across pairs of states from 1875 to 2002. The fitted relationship differed by regime type. The authors interpreted the pattern as evidence about changes in leaders' risk-taking with age.

headline: Are leaders who served in the military without seeing combat more likely to start disputes?
title: How Prior Military Experience Influences the Future Militarized Behavior of Leaders
note: The authors compared military biographies of more than 2,500 heads of state with records of dispute initiation. They found higher initiation rates among leaders with military service but no combat experience and among former rebels, and used the pattern to infer how background shapes decisions in office.

headline: Can the outcomes of assassination attempts explain which political institutions change?
title: Hit or Miss? The Effect of Assassinations on Institutions and War
note: The authors compared institutional and conflict outcomes after successful and failed assassination attempts recorded from 1875 to 2004. Their interpretation uses variation in whether an attempt succeeded to estimate the effects of removing a leader.

headline: Can a leader's death in office reveal their effect on economic growth?
title: Do Leaders Matter? National Leadership and Growth Since World War II
note: The authors used deaths in office from natural causes or accidents as a source of leadership transitions and compared growth before and after. They interpreted breaks in growth rates around the transitions as evidence about the influence of national leaders.

headline: Can the grammar of the language you are surveyed in change your support for long-term policy?
title: Language Shapes People's Time Perspective and Support for Future-Oriented Policies
note: Estonian-Russian bilinguals were randomly assigned to answer in one language. The authors used differences in expressed support for policies with a future time horizon to infer a role for how the languages mark future tense.

headline: Can a Swedish pronoun change what people say about equality?
title: Language influences mass opinion toward gender and LGBT equality
note: Three experiments in Sweden compared use of a gender-neutral pronoun with gendered forms. The authors related differences in whom participants brought to mind and in their stated attitudes to a proposed effect of language on public opinion.

headline: Can ancestral plough use explain why fewer women participate in politics today?
title: On the Origins of Gender Roles: Women and the Plough
note: The authors linked historical plough use to contemporary outcomes, including women's participation in politics. Some analyses used historical crop suitability to predict plough adoption. The study interpreted those relationships as evidence that farming practices left lasting gender norms.

headline: Can a government payroll show which jobs go to political allies and which go to bureaucrats' contacts?
title: Who Gets Hired? Political Patronage and Bureaucratic Favoritism
note: The authors modeled how politicians and bureaucratic managers compete to influence hiring and tested its predictions with Kenyan local-government payrolls. They used patterns across job types to infer the relative roles of patronage and bureaucratic favoritism.

headline: Can oil production explain why women hold fewer political offices in some countries?
title: Oil, Islam, and Women
note: The study related oil production to women's employment and political representation and compared Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia. It proposed that changes in employment opportunities help explain how oil production relates to political representation.

headline: Does describing a protest as mostly women change how much repression people think it deserves?
title: The Effect of Protesters’ Gender on Public Reactions to Protests and Protest Repression
note: The author varied protesters' gender composition and descriptions in a survey experiment. Respondents rated perceived violence, credibility, and whether repression was warranted. The study used those judgments to infer how gender stereotypes affect support for repression.

headline: Does your skin conductance reveal whether you see a political issue as a moral one?
title: Fired Up by Morality: The Unique Physiological Response Tied to Moral Conviction in Politics
note: The study compared self-reported moral conviction with skin conductance during exposure to political stimuli. The author interpreted arousal differences as evidence that moral conviction involves a distinctive form of emotional processing.

headline: Does a national football win make people report less attachment to their ethnic group?
title: Building Nations Through Shared Experiences: Evidence From African Football
note: The authors compared survey responses around international matches and used close qualification outcomes to study conflict. They interpreted some changes as evidence that shared football experiences strengthen national identification.

headline: Does a football win get the president better approval ratings?
title: The Political Relevance of Irrelevant Events
note: The authors reported a short-lived effect of a football game outcome on presidential approval in an experiment. A later study by two of the authors reproduced the result on a limited set of outcomes. https://doi.org/10.1017/XPS.2017.22

headline: When your candidate loses, does your testosterone drop too?
title: Dominance, Politics, and Physiology: Voters’ Testosterone Changes on the Night of the 2008 United States Presidential Election
note: Researchers collected voters' saliva on the night of the 2008 US presidential election. After the result came in, testosterone fell among men who had backed a losing candidate and held roughly steady among men who had voted for Obama.

headline: Flash “RATS” on a screen. Does a candidate look worse?
title: RATS, We Should Have Used Clinton: Subliminal Priming in Political Campaigns
note: In an online experiment inspired by a 2000 campaign ad, participants exposed to the masked word RATS gave more negative ratings to an unfamiliar hypothetical candidate. The outcome was a candidate rating.

headline: Dry Fourths of July as a kid, more Republican votes as an adult?
title: Shaping the Nation: The Effect of Fourth of July on Political Preferences and Behavior in the United States
venue: Harvard Kennedy School Faculty Research Working Paper Series
note: The authors used local Fourth of July rainfall to estimate whether children attended celebrations. They then examined the link between holiday weather during childhood and voting preferences in adulthood.

headline: Can narrowly qualifying for the World Cup predict more disputes between countries?
title: Nationalism and Conflict: Lessons From International Sports
note: The study used close qualification outcomes to estimate whether World Cup participation shifted subsequent interstate disputes and interpreted the pattern in terms of nationalism.

headline: Could a rainstorm have changed the Brexit vote?
title: Could rainfall have swung the result of the Brexit referendum?
note: The authors used rainfall and local referendum results to estimate changes in Leave and Remain votes associated with rain.

headline: Can wind speed change how people vote?
title: The Impact of Incidental Environmental Factors on Vote Choice: Wind Speed is Related to More Prevention-Focused Voting
note: The authors reported an association between election-day wind speed and prevention-oriented voting choices.

headline: Do winning sports teams help reelect mayors?
title: For the Win! The Effect of Professional Sports Records on Mayoral Elections
note: The paper related professional sports teams’ records to mayoral elections. The estimated relationship with incumbent votes was larger than the one reported for local unemployment in the same analysis.

headline: Do legislators use simpler language on hotter days?
title: The Effect of Temperature on Language Complexity: Evidence From Seven Million Parliamentary Speeches
note: The authors matched historical weather records to parliamentary speeches and used textual measures of language complexity. Several estimates linked hotter days with simpler speech.

headline: Can the length of the old telephone line help explain who turns out to vote?
title: E-lections: Voting Behavior and the Internet
note: The authors used technical constraints in the German telephone network as a source of variation in broadband availability. They estimated a decline in turnout and examined changes in media use.

headline: Can living near a wind turbine change which party gets blamed at the ballot box?
title: Electoral Backlash Against Climate Policy: A Natural Experiment on Retrospective Voting and Local Resistance to Public Policy
note: The author compared electoral shifts near wind projects with shifts elsewhere and reported a local penalty for the incumbent party associated with the projects.

headline: Do opposing political parties literally look disgusting?
title: Disgusting Democrats and Repulsive Republicans: Members of Political Outgroups Are Considered Physically Gross
note: The authors found differences in reported disgust toward political opponents, but no corresponding difference on their nonverbal facial-expression measure.

headline: Can't stand body odor? What does that say about your politics?
title: Body odour disgust sensitivity predicts authoritarian attitudes
note: Participants answered questionnaires about body odor and authoritarian attitudes. Across two studies, the authors found that people who rated body odor as more disgusting also scored higher on the authoritarianism scale.

headline: Can your eyes reveal your politics when you see a disgusted face?
title: Is that disgust I see? Political ideology and biased visual attention
note: The authors associated socially conservative attitudes with greater visual attention to disgusted faces and less attention to neutral faces.

headline: Do tidy people become more politically conservative?
title: An orderly personality partially explains the link between trait disgust and political conservatism
note: The paper investigates orderliness as a statistical mediator of the association between disgust and ideology.

headline: Does questioning men’s masculinity make liberals favor tougher politicians?
title: Something to Prove? Manhood Threats Increase Political Aggression Among Liberal Men
note: The authors reported that experimentally threatening men’s sense of masculinity increased preference for aggressive political policies or candidates among liberal men across their experiments. The outcomes differ from those in Willer et al. (2013).

headline: Are conservative politicians better-looking?
title: The right look: Conservative politicians look better and voters reward it
note: Photographic appearance ratings were linked to political orientation and electoral outcomes across datasets.

headline: Can physical attractiveness predict people's political beliefs?
title: Effects of physical attractiveness on political beliefs
note: The study investigated associations between assessed attractiveness and political attitudes.

headline: How much of the similarity in political opinions between twins gets attributed to genetic differences?
title: Are Political Orientations Genetically Transmitted?
note: The authors compared identical and fraternal twins on political attitude items and used a model to partition variation into genetic and environmental components.

headline: Can turnout records from twins yield an estimate of how heritable voting is?
title: Genetic Variation in Political Participation
note: The authors compared the resemblance of identical and fraternal twins on turnout and other participation measures and used the difference to estimate a genetic contribution.

headline: Can a model of twins’ fearfulness help account for who opposes immigrants or other groups?
title: Fear as a Disposition and an Emotional State: A Genetic and Environmental Approach to Out-Group Political Preferences
note: The authors fitted models to twin data and examined effects of a fear manipulation in separate data to distinguish dispositional and situational associations with outgroup attitudes.

headline: Can presidential election results be predicted from the candidates' voices?
title: Vocal characteristics of presidential candidates can predict the outcome of actual elections
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can the pitch of a candidate's voice predict actual election results?
title: Candidate Voice Pitch Influences Election Outcomes
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does a deeper voice help presidential candidates in conservative countries?
title: Presidential, But Not Prime Minister, Candidates With Lower Pitched Voices Stand a Better Chance of Winning the Election in Conservative Countries
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can a candidate's voice tip the vote despite policy differences?
title: Persistence of voice pitch bias against policy differences
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Do voters prefer a lower-pitched candidate?
title: Voice pitch influences voting behavior
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Same campaign pitch. Does the lower voice win?
title: Sounds like a winner: voice pitch influences perception of leadership capacity in both men and women
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
note: Researchers raised or lowered the pitch of the same recorded appeal for votes. When listeners chose between the two versions, they more often picked the lower voice, for both male and female speakers.

headline: Do conservatives prefer candidates with dominant-looking faces?
title: Winning Faces Vary by Ideology: How Nonverbal Source Cues Influence Election and Communication Success in Politics
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can a politician's face affect who gets nominated by their party?
title: When the Party Decides: The Effects of Facial Competence and Dominance on Internal Nominations of Political Candidates
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Do attractive-looking candidates seem to belong to a particular ideology?
title: Attractiveness and Facial Competence Bias Face-Based Inferences of Candidate Ideology
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can a good-looking candidate win more votes?
title: The looks of a winner: Beauty and electoral success
note: Photograph-based beauty ratings were compared with election results of Finnish political candidates.

headline: Does television make less-informed voters more likely to favor better-looking candidates?
title: Looking the Part: Television Leads Less Informed Citizens to Vote Based on Candidates’ Appearance
note: The authors combined ratings of candidate appearance with voter knowledge, television exposure, and vote choices to estimate when the appearance association was strongest.

headline: Can a glimpse of the Confederate flag cost Obama support in a survey?
title: How Exposure to the Confederate Flag Affects Willingness to Vote for Barack Obama
note: An experiment reported lower stated willingness to vote for Obama after exposure to a Confederate flag compared with a neutral symbol. The study also tested ratings of a hypothetical target in a separate experiment.

topic: Winning Votes and Turning Out Voters
headline: Was Oprah's endorsement worth a million votes?
title: Can Celebrity Endorsements Affect Political Outcomes? Evidence from the 2008 US Democratic Presidential Primary
venue: The Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization
note: The authors used local subscriptions to Oprah's magazine and sales of her book picks to estimate her influence. They calculated that her endorsement brought Barack Obama roughly a million extra votes in the Democratic presidential primary.

headline: Can sharing a last name with a local candidate win you votes?
title: Share the Name, Share the Vote: A Natural Experiment of Name Recognition
note: In elections for Japan's upper house, a candidate on the national proportional-representation ballot tended to win a larger share of votes in prefectures where a local candidate happened to have the same surname.

headline: Should Republicans hope for rain on Election Day?
title: The Republicans Should Pray for Rain: Weather, Turnout, and Voting in U.S. Presidential Elections
note: The authors matched county-level returns from 14 US presidential elections with local weather records. They reported lower turnout and a higher Republican share of the vote in rain or snow.

headline: Does voting in a school make school funding more popular?
title: Contextual priming: Where people vote affects how they vote
note: An Arizona school-funding measure drew a higher share of yes votes at polling places located in schools. The authors also ran an experiment showing participants pictures of schools.

headline: Does voting in a church change how people vote on same-sex marriage?
title: Deus Ex Machina: The Influence of Polling Place on Voting Behavior
note: Rutchick reported that precincts using churches as polling sites showed more support for a ballot measure banning same-sex marriage. The paper also reports a field experiment on church cues and attitudes.

headline: Can a candidate's luck start with a letter drawn from a hat?
title: Estimating Causal Effects of Ballot Order from a Randomized Natural Experiment: The California Alphabet Lottery, 1978–2002
note: California draws letters to set the order of names on the ballot. In elections from 1978 to 2002, the authors found an advantage for candidates listed first in primaries. In general elections, they detected an order effect only for minor-party candidates.

headline: Can disgust sensitivity predict which party people vote for?
title: Disgust Sensitivity, Political Conservatism, and Voting
note: The authors related disgust sensitivity to ideology and reported voting behavior.

headline: Can encountering Spanish-speaking commuters change how others answer immigration questions?
title: Causal Effect of Intergroup Contact on Exclusionary Attitudes
note: The researcher assigned Spanish-speaking confederates to commuter platforms and compared survey responses across exposure conditions, reporting more exclusionary attitudes after repeated contact.

headline: Can a radio soap opera make listeners more willing to dispute a group decision?
title: Deference, Dissent, and Dispute Resolution: An Experimental Intervention Using Mass Media to Change Norms and Behavior in Rwanda
note: Rwandan communities listened to different radio programs. The authors compared reported norms and observed group behavior, finding changes in several forms of dissent and cooperation.

headline: Does where a news channel sits on a cable lineup help predict how viewers vote?
title: Bias in Cable News: Persuasion and Polarization
note: The authors used variation in cable channel positions to estimate changes in viewing and linked those shifts to voting through a model of persuasion and channel choice.

headline: Did the arrival of television push voters away from the polls?
title: Television and Voter Turnout
note: The author compared markets as television arrived at different times and estimated lower turnout, especially in off-year elections, alongside declines in use of other news sources.

headline: Can a television signal shift enough votes to matter in a national election?
title: Media and Political Persuasion: Evidence From Russia
note: The authors related geographic access to independent television to 1999 election results and survey reports, estimating reduced support for the government party where the signal was available.

headline: Could radio reception help explain where participation in mass violence was greater?
title: Propaganda and Conflict: Evidence From the Rwandan Genocide
note: The author used terrain-based variation in radio reception and village-level prosecution records to estimate a link between propaganda exposure and participation in violence.

headline: Did greater radio access predict opposite voting responses as broadcast control changed?
title: Radio and the Rise of the Nazis in Prewar Germany
note: The authors combined geography-based radio coverage estimates with historical election returns and reported opposite associations before and after radio content shifted in favor of the Nazis.

headline: Can watching entertainment TV before a channel carries political news predict a vote years later?
title: The Political Legacy of Entertainment TV
note: The authors used geographic variation in early access to Berlusconi’s entertainment channels and reported shifts in later support for his party and a subsequent populist party.

headline: Can showing friends’ faces next to an “I Voted” button change real turnout?
title: A 61-Million-Person Experiment in Social Influence and Political Mobilization
note: Facebook randomly varied election-day messages, including whether they showed friends who had clicked a voting button. The authors linked a subset of users to turnout records and reported a small increase for the social message.

headline: Does barely winning an election make your relatives more likely to enter Congress?
title: Political Dynasties
note: The authors combined Congressional family histories and close-election comparisons to estimate whether an elected politician’s tenure increased the chance that relatives later served in Congress.

headline: Can a party label affect who gets a scholarship in a test decision?
title: Fear and Loathing Across Party Lines: New Evidence on Group Polarization
note: The authors varied categories such as race or party in applicant profiles and compared selections. The partisan contrast was large in some conditions.

headline: Does political compatibility show up in who messages whom on a dating site?
title: Political Homophily in Social Relationships: Evidence From Online Dating Behavior
note: The authors combined dating-site behavior with an experiment on profiles to estimate how political similarity was related to contact and interest.

headline: Can a free subscription change voting even when the newspaper endorses the other party?
title: Does the Media Matter? A Field Experiment Measuring the Effect of Newspapers on Voting Behavior and Political Opinions
note: Households were given subscriptions to either of two newspapers or neither. The authors found suggestive shifts toward the Democratic candidate in the survey regardless of which newspaper was assigned.

headline: Can publishing a corruption audit change an election more where there is local radio?
title: Exposing Corrupt Politicians: The Effects of Brazil’s Publicly Released Audits on Electoral Outcomes
note: Brazil selected municipalities for audit by lottery. The authors compared electoral responses to disclosed corruption and found a larger response where local radio could carry the news.

headline: Do some people vote so they can honestly tell a stranger that they voted?
title: Voting to Tell Others
note: Door-to-door experiments varied whether households expected to be asked about voting. The authors used turnout and survey responses to model the social value of reporting that one voted.

headline: Can showing people an existing poll move them toward the candidate already in front?
title: Off the Fence, Onto the Bandwagon? A Large-Scale Survey Experiment on Effect of Real-Life Poll Outcomes on Subsequent Vote Intentions
venue: International Journal of Public Opinion Research
note: The authors varied exposure to real polling figures and measured subsequent stated vote intentions, estimating a small shift toward some parties shown gaining support.

headline: Will voters choose a candidate from their party who says they would bend election rules?
title: Democracy in America? Partisanship, Polarization, and the Robustness of Support for Democracy in the United States
note: Candidate-choice experiments varied party, policy and democratic conduct. The authors estimated how often voters were willing to trade democratic principles for other valued candidate traits.

headline: Can people agree the economy has deteriorated and still shift blame to protect their party?
title: Bias Will Find a Way: Economic Perceptions, Attributions of Blame, and Partisan-Motivated Reasoning During Crisis
note: Survey analyses compared perceived economic conditions with responsibility judgments. Partisan differences could persist in blame even when evaluations of conditions converged.

headline: Can changing the party label on the same welfare plan reverse people’s judgments of it?
title: Party Over Policy: The Dominating Impact of Group Influence on Political Beliefs
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researcher varied welfare-policy details and which party ostensibly endorsed them. Participants’ ratings moved strongly with that party attribution.

headline: Can exposure to Chinese imports predict which places move toward more ideologically extreme candidates?
title: Importing Political Polarization? The Electoral Consequences of Rising Trade Exposure
note: The authors linked local exposure to import competition to electoral returns and congressional voting records, reporting different partisan shifts across local demographic compositions.

headline: Did precincts closer to the 1992 Los Angeles riot shift their votes toward spending on public goods?
title: Can Violent Protest Change Local Policy Support? Evidence From the Aftermath of the 1992 Los Angeles Riot
note: The authors compared voting patterns around the riot and reported a local shift in support for public spending measures.

headline: Did different protest tactics shift newspaper coverage toward civil rights or toward public order?
title: Agenda Seeding: How 1960s Black Protests Moved Elites, Public Opinion and Voting
note: The author linked protest event records to news coverage, public opinion and voting. The estimates differed between nonviolent protests and episodes involving protester violence.

headline: Does swapping an algorithmic feed for a chronological one change political opinions?
title: How Do Social Media Feed Algorithms Affect Attitudes and Behavior in an Election Campaign?
note: Facebook and Instagram users were randomly assigned to chronological feeds. The change affected content exposure and use, while the study found no detectable effects on several political attitudes.

headline: Does automatically mailing ballots to everyone give one party a measurable advantage?
title: Universal Vote-by-Mail Has No Impact on Partisan Turnout or Vote Share
note: Comparing staggered policy changes across counties, the authors estimated a modest increase in overall turnout without a detectable shift in the parties’ relative turnout or vote shares.

topic: Who people picture when they rate a party
headline: Does asking about ordinary voters instead of parties change the measured size of partisan hostility?
title: “(Mis)estimating” Affective Polarization
note: Survey experiments varied whether respondents evaluated parties, elites, or ordinary voters. The authors found that the choice of target changed the measured gap.

headline: Can people feel less hostile toward the other party without becoming more supportive of democracy?
title: Interventions Reducing Affective Polarization Do Not Necessarily Improve Anti-Democratic Attitudes
note: The authors compared experimental outcomes on partisan dislike with outcomes on support for political violence or undemocratic practices and found that improvement on the former did not reliably carry over.

headline: Does refugee placement predict opposite electoral shifts in urban and less urban areas?
title: Refugee Migration and Electoral Outcomes
note: Using a Danish placement policy, the authors estimated electoral responses to refugee arrivals. The direction of the estimate differed between large cities and less urban municipalities.

headline: Can a town respond differently to refugees passing through than to refugees settling there?
title: Contact Versus Exposure: Refugee Presence and Voting for the Far Right
note: The study compared Austrian municipalities with different experiences of refugee arrivals. It reported opposite estimated shifts in far-right voting for transit exposure and longer-term local hosting.

headline: Can a Greek island’s proximity to a refugee route change residents’ political attitudes?
title: Does Exposure to the Refugee Crisis Make Natives More Hostile?
note: The researchers compared residents of Greek islands with different exposure to refugee arrivals and found higher hostility in survey responses from more exposed islands.

headline: Do voters reward disaster relief more than spending that prevents damage?
title: Myopic Voters and Natural Disaster Policy
note: County-level spending and voting records were used to estimate electoral returns to disaster relief and preparedness. The authors reported a reward for relief spending and little evidence of one for preparedness.

headline: Did flood relief buy the German incumbent party years of electoral goodwill?
title: How Lasting Is Voter Gratitude? An Analysis of the Short- and Long-Term Electoral Returns to Beneficial Policy
note: Comparing German areas differentially affected by the 2002 flood, the authors estimated a seven-point incumbent advantage in the immediate election and a smaller advantage in the next election.

headline: Who gets blamed for a flood when the weather is beyond their control?
title: Who Is Held Responsible When Disaster Strikes? The Attribution of Responsibility for a Natural Disaster in an Urban Election
note: The authors linked Houston survey and election evidence to perceptions of responsibility after flooding, distinguishing disaster exposure from evaluations of the government response.

headline: Can a single get-out-the-vote campaign create voters who return the following year?
title: Voting May Be Habit-Forming: Evidence From a Randomized Field Experiment
note: The authors compared later turnout records between voters randomly assigned to mobilization and control conditions in an earlier election and interpreted the sustained difference as habit formation.

headline: Can saying that many people will vote be more motivating than warning that turnout will be low?
title: Descriptive Social Norms and Motivation to Vote: Everybody’s Voting and So Should You
note: Two field experiments compared reactions to high- and low-turnout messages. The authors reported greater motivation following high-turnout messages.

headline: Can asking voters when and how they will get to the polls change whether they go?
title: Do You Have a Voting Plan? Implementation Intentions, Voter Turnout, and Organic Plan Making
note: A randomized field experiment compared turnout records across phone scripts, including one that prompted respondents to plan the time and logistics of voting.

headline: Can a single doorstep conversation change prejudice ratings months later?
title: Durably Reducing Transphobia: A Field Experiment on Door-to-Door Canvassing
note: Households were randomly assigned to different canvassing conversations. The researchers compared repeated survey measures and reported an attitude difference that persisted for months.

headline: Did adding Fox News to a cable lineup change Republican vote share?
title: The Fox News Effect: Media Bias and Voting
note: The authors compared changes in election returns across towns that did and did not gain Fox News access. They reported a small but measurable increase in Republican vote share in towns gaining access.

headline: Can Russian television reception shift election results across the border in Ukraine?
title: Electoral Effects of Biased Media: Russian Television in Ukraine
note: The authors related predicted Russian television reception to Ukrainian electoral returns and survey responses, reporting greater support for pro-Russian parties in some settings.

headline: Will voters accept a policy that cuts against their ideology if their party’s leader endorses it?
title: Does Party Trump Ideology? Disentangling Party and Ideology in America
note: Survey experiments crossed policy positions with attribution to Donald Trump. Some respondents moved toward his stated position even when it departed from the usual ideological direction.

headline: Can the opposition’s endorsement turn people against the very same policy?
title: Polarizing Cues
note: Survey experiments varied whether a named political figure endorsed a proposal. Endorsements by opposing-party figures often reduced support.

topic: Winning Votes and Turning Out Voters
headline: Would you vote if the neighbors could see whether you showed up?
title: Social Pressure and Voter Turnout: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
note: In a Michigan field experiment, researchers mailed different turnout reminders. People were more likely to vote after receiving a letter saying their family or neighbors would be told whether they went to the polls.

headline: Does moving a marginalized candidate higher on a randomized ballot change who wins?
title: Alphabet Soup: Randomized Ballot Order and the Representation of Marginalized Candidates
note: The authors used randomly assigned ballot order to estimate differential effects on candidate performance and representation.

headline: Does being listed first give New York candidates extra votes?
title: The Effects of Ballot Position on Election Outcomes
note: The authors used randomized candidate order across precincts in New York City primaries to estimate how much the first position changed vote shares.

headline: Do voters substitute the last year of an administration for the entire term when judging its economic record?
title: Substituting the End for the Whole: Why Voters Respond Primarily to the Election-Year Economy
note: Survey experiments varied what economic information respondents received. The authors found that providing cumulative performance information reduced the disproportionate weight of the final year.
